units.title: Hello, Lua!
units.summary: Write your first Lua program, print text and numbers, and calculate with the basic math operators.

lesson.md: Lua is a small and fast programming language. Many games, apps and tools use it to run scripts. A Lua program is a text file whose name ends in `.lua`. You run it in a terminal with the command `lua hello.lua`.

lesson.code: print("Hello, Lua!")

lesson.md: `print` is a **function**: a named piece of code that does a job. You call it with parentheses `()`. The value inside the parentheses is the **argument**. `print` writes it on the screen and then starts a new line.
Text in quotes is a **string**. You can use double quotes `"` or single quotes `'`; both make the same string. Lua runs the lines of a program from top to bottom.

lesson.code:
print("Hello")
print("World")
print('Single quotes work too')
lesson.output:
Hello
World
Single quotes work too

lesson.md: Numbers have no quotes. Lua knows the operators `+` (plus), `-` (minus), `*` (times) and `/` (divided by). As in math, `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses `()` decide what Lua calculates first.

lesson.code:
print(2 + 3)
print(10 - 4)
print(6 * 7)
print(2 + 3 * 4)
print((2 + 3) * 4)

lesson.md: Lua has two kinds of numbers: **integers** are whole numbers such as `7`, and **floats** have a decimal point, such as `3.5`. The `/` operator always gives a float, even when the result is a whole number. `//` divides and rounds down to a whole number, `%` gives the remainder of a division, and `^` raises a number to a power.

lesson.code:
print(7 / 2)
print(6 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(7 % 2)
print(2 ^ 3)

lesson.md: Look closely at the results: `6 / 2` prints `3.0`, not `3`. A float always shows a decimal point. `^` also always gives a float, so `2 ^ 3` is `8.0`.
Two dashes `--` start a **comment**. Lua ignores everything from `--` to the end of the line. In this course, comments only show results, like `-- 2`.

card: `print("Hi")` writes a line on the screen
Strings go in quotes: `"text"` or `'text'`
`//` divides and rounds down, `%` is the remainder, `^` is a power
`--` starts a comment; run a file with `lua file.lua`

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in local variables, and meet the types number, string, boolean and nil and the type() function.

lesson.md: A **variable** is a name for a value. You create one with the keyword `local`, a name, the equals sign `=` and a value. Here `=` means "store this value", not "is equal to". After that, the name stands for the value.

lesson.code:
local name = "Mia"
local age = 12
print(name)
print(age)

lesson.md: You can give a variable a new value later. Write `local` only the first time; after that, use the name and `=`. Lua calculates the right side first, so `score = score + 5` adds `5` to the old value.

lesson.code:
local score = 10
score = score + 5
print(score)
score = score * 2
print(score)

lesson.md: Names may contain letters, digits and `_`, but they cannot start with a digit. Lua is **case-sensitive**: `age` and `Age` are two different variables. Some words, such as `local`, `end` and `if`, are **keywords** and cannot be names.
Without `local`, you create a **global** variable that every part of the program can see and change. This causes mistakes that are hard to find. Always use `local` for new variables.
You can create several variables in one line: `local a, b = 1, 2`. The first name gets the first value, the second name gets the second value.

Every value has a **type**. The function `type()` returns the name of the type as a string. Integers and floats both have the type `number`, text has the type `string`, and the two values `true` and `false` have the type `boolean`.

lesson.code:
print(type(42))
print(type(3.14))
print(type("hi"))
print(type(true))

lesson.md: `nil` is a special value that means "no value". A variable that you create without a value is `nil`. The type of `nil` is also called `nil`.

lesson.code:
local x
print(x)
print(type(x))

lesson.md: `tostring()` turns a value into a string, and `tonumber()` turns a string into a number. If the string does not contain a number, `tonumber()` returns `nil`.

lesson.code:
local text = "42"
local n = tonumber(text)
print(n + 8)
print(type(tostring(5)))
print(tonumber("hello"))

card: `local x = 5` creates a variable; `x = x + 1` changes it
`local a, b = 1, 2` creates two variables
`type(x)` returns `"number"`, `"string"`, `"boolean"` or `"nil"`
`nil` means no value; a new variable without a value is `nil`
`tonumber("42")` gives `42`, `tostring(5)` gives `"5"`

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Join strings with .., measure them with #, and change them with string.upper, string.sub, string.rep and string.format.

lesson.md: The operator `..` (two dots) joins two strings into one. This is called **concatenation**. When you join a number with a string, Lua turns the number into text.

lesson.code:
local first = "Ada"
local last = "Lovelace"
print(first .. " " .. last)
print("Age: " .. 36)

lesson.md: Put `#` before a string to get its **length**: the number of characters. Spaces count too.

lesson.code:
local word = "Lua"
print(#word)
print(#"Hello world")

lesson.md: `#` counts bytes, not letters. Letters such as `é` or `ü` take two bytes, so `#"é"` is `2`. With plain English letters, one letter is one byte.

Lua keeps its string functions in the **string library**. You call them with `string`, a dot `.` and the name of the function. `string.upper(s)` returns `s` in capital letters, `string.lower(s)` in small letters, and `string.rep(s, n)` repeats `s` `n` times.

lesson.code:
local s = "Hello"
print(string.upper(s))
print(string.lower(s))
print(string.rep("ab", 3))
print(s)

lesson.md: These functions return a new string. They never change the original string, as the last line above shows. Store the result when you need it: `s = string.upper(s)`.

`string.sub(s, i, j)` returns the part of `s` from position `i` to position `j`, both included. The first character has the position `1`. A negative position counts from the end: `-1` is the last character. Without `j`, the part goes to the end of the string.

lesson.code:
local word = "programming"
print(string.sub(word, 1, 3))
print(string.sub(word, 4, 7))
print(string.sub(word, -3))
print(string.sub(word, 8))

lesson.md: `string.format` builds a string from a pattern. In the pattern, `%s` stands for any value as text, `%d` for a whole number, and `%.2f` for a number with two digits after the decimal point. The values follow the pattern, in the same order.

lesson.code:
local name = "Tom"
local items = 3
local total = 7.5
print(string.format("%s bought %d items.", name, items))
print(string.format("Total: %.2f", total))

card: `"a" .. "b"` joins strings: `"ab"`
`#s` is the length of `s`
`string.upper(s)`, `string.lower(s)`, `string.rep(s, n)`
`string.sub(s, 2, 4)` takes characters 2 to 4; `-1` is the last one
`string.format("%s has %d", name, n)`; `%.2f` shows two decimals

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Run code only when a condition is true with if, elseif and else, and combine conditions with and, or and not.

lesson.md: A **comparison** checks two values and gives a boolean: `true` or `false`. `==` means "is equal to", `~=` means "is not equal to", and `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=` compare sizes. Remember: `=` stores a value, `==` compares two values.

lesson.code:
print(5 > 3)
print(5 == 3)
print(5 ~= 3)
print("a" == "a")
print(10 <= 10)

lesson.md: `if` runs code only when a condition is true. Write `if`, the condition, `then`, the code and `end`. The code between `then` and `end` is a **block**. Indent it with 4 spaces so that it is easy to read.

lesson.code:
local temp = 30
if temp > 25 then
    print("It is hot.")
end
print("Done.")

lesson.md: `else` adds a block that runs when the condition is false. `elseif` checks another condition. Lua tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true. One `end` closes the whole `if`.

lesson.code:
local score = 72
if score >= 90 then
    print("A")
elseif score >= 70 then
    print("B")
else
    print("C")
end

lesson.md: `elseif` is one word. `else if` with a space starts a new `if` inside the `else` block, and that `if` needs its own `end`.
`and` is true when both sides are true. `or` is true when at least one side is true. `not` turns `true` into `false` and `false` into `true`.

lesson.code:
local age = 15
local hasTicket = true
print(age >= 12 and hasTicket)
print(age < 12 or age > 65)
print(not hasTicket)

lesson.md: In a condition, only `false` and `nil` count as false. Every other value counts as true, also the number `0` and the empty string `""`.

lesson.code:
if 0 then
    print("0 counts as true")
end
if nil then
    print("nil counts as true")
else
    print("nil counts as false")
end
lesson.output:
0 counts as true
nil counts as false

lesson.md: `or` returns the first value that counts as true. So `name or "guest"` gives `name` when it has a value, and `"guest"` when `name` is `nil`. This is a common way to set a default value.

card: `if x > 0 then ... elseif x < 0 then ... else ... end`
`and`, `or` and `not` combine conditions
Only `false` and `nil` count as false; `0` and `""` count as true
`name or "guest"` gives a default value

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with the numeric for loop, while and repeat ... until, and stop a loop early with break.

lesson.md: A **loop** repeats code. The numeric `for` loop counts: `for i = 1, 5 do` sets `i` to `1`, `2`, `3`, `4` and `5`, one after the other, and runs the block between `do` and `end` once for each value. The end value is included.

lesson.code:
for i = 1, 3 do
    print("Round " .. i)
end

lesson.md: A third number sets the **step**: how much `i` changes each time. Without it, the step is `1`. A negative step counts down.

lesson.code:
for i = 0, 10, 5 do
    print(i)
end
for i = 3, 1, -1 do
    print(i)
end

lesson.md: Loops often build a result step by step. Create a variable before the loop and change it inside the loop. After the loop, the variable holds the result.

lesson.code:
local sum = 0
for i = 1, 4 do
    sum = sum + i
end
print(sum)

lesson.md: The loop variable `i` is local to the loop: it only exists between `do` and `end`. Do not change it inside the loop; use another variable for your own values.
A `while` loop repeats its block as long as its condition is true. Lua checks the condition before each round. Make sure the block changes something in the condition, or the loop never stops.

lesson.code:
local n = 1
while n < 50 do
    n = n * 3
end
print(n)

lesson.md: `repeat ... until` checks the condition after each round, so the block always runs at least once. The loop stops as soon as the condition is true.

lesson.code:
local count = 0
repeat
    count = count + 1
    print(count)
until count >= 3

lesson.md: `break` stops a loop at once. The program continues after the `end` of the loop.

lesson.code:
for i = 1, 10 do
    if i * i > 20 then
        break
    end
    print(i)
end
print("stop")

card: `for i = 1, 5 do ... end` counts from 1 to 5
`for i = 10, 0, -2 do` counts down in steps of 2
`while cond do ... end` checks before each round
`repeat ... until cond` runs at least once
`break` leaves the loop at once

units.title: Functions
units.summary: Write your own functions, return one or more values, accept any number of arguments and use functions as values.

lesson.md: A **function** is a named block of code that you can run again and again. Write `local function`, a name, the **parameters** in parentheses, the block and `end`. Parameters are variables that get their values from the call. As with variables, `local` keeps the function local.

lesson.code:
local function greet(name)
    print("Hello, " .. name .. "!")
end

greet("Ana")
greet("Ben")

lesson.md: `return` sends a value back to the caller. The call then stands for that value, so you can store it or use it in a calculation. Define a function before the line that calls it.

lesson.code:
local function square(n)
    return n * n
end

local result = square(4)
print(result)
print(square(3) + 1)

lesson.md: When you pass fewer arguments than there are parameters, the missing parameters are `nil`. Together with `or`, this gives you default values.

lesson.code:
local function hello(name)
    name = name or "friend"
    print("Hi, " .. name)
end

hello("Lea")
hello()

lesson.md: A function can return several values, separated by commas. To get them, write several variables on the left side of `=`.

lesson.code:
local function minMax(a, b)
    if a < b then
        return a, b
    end
    return b, a
end

local low, high = minMax(8, 3)
print(low)
print(high)

lesson.md: Three dots `...` as the last parameter accept any number of arguments. `select("#", ...)` gives the number of arguments, and `select(i, ...)` gives the argument at position `i`.

lesson.code:
local function sum(...)
    local total = 0
    for i = 1, select("#", ...) do
        total = total + select(i, ...)
    end
    return total
end

print(sum(1, 2, 3))
print(sum(10, 20))
print(sum())

lesson.md: A function is a value, like a number or a string. You can store it in a variable and pass it to another function. `function(x) ... end` without a name creates an **anonymous function**.

lesson.code:
local function apply(f, x)
    return f(x)
end

local double = function(x)
    return x * 2
end

print(apply(double, 5))
print(apply(function(x) return x + 1 end, 5))
print(type(double))

card: `local function add(a, b) return a + b end`
Missing arguments are `nil`: `name = name or "friend"`
`return a, b` returns two values: `local x, y = f()`
`...` accepts any number of arguments; `select("#", ...)` counts them
Functions are values: `local f = function(x) return x * 2 end`

    return select("#", ...)

print(count("a", "b", "c"))

units.title: Tables as lists
units.summary: Keep many values in one table: read them by position, count them with #, loop with ipairs, and add, remove and join items.

lesson.md: A **table** holds many values. It is the only data structure in Lua. Write the values between braces `{}`, separated by commas. A table like this is a **list**: each value has a position, called its **index**.

lesson.code:
local fruits = {"apple", "banana", "cherry"}
print(fruits[1])
print(fruits[3])
print(#fruits)

lesson.md: In Lua, the first index is `1`, not `0` as in many other languages. `t[i]` reads the value at index `i`, `#t` gives the length of the list, and `t[i] = v` changes a value. An index without a value gives `nil`.

lesson.code:
local nums = {10, 20, 30}
print(nums[0])
print(nums[#nums])
nums[2] = 25
print(nums[2])

lesson.md: A numeric `for` loop from `1` to `#t` visits every index. Shorter is `ipairs`: `for i, v in ipairs(t) do` gives you the index `i` and the value `v` of each item, in order.

lesson.code:
local colors = {"red", "green", "blue"}
for i = 1, #colors do
    print(colors[i])
end
for i, color in ipairs(colors) do
    print(i .. ": " .. color)
end
lesson.output:
red
green
blue
1: red
2: green
3: blue

lesson.md: When you do not need the index, call it `_`: `for _, v in ipairs(t) do`. `_` is a normal variable name, but it tells readers that the value is not used.
`table.insert(t, v)` adds `v` at the end of the list. `table.insert(t, 1, v)` adds it at index `1` and moves the other items up. `table.remove(t)` removes the last item and returns it.

lesson.code:
local list = {"b", "c"}
table.insert(list, "d")
table.insert(list, 1, "a")
print(#list)
local last = table.remove(list)
print(last)
print(#list)

lesson.md: `table.concat(t, sep)` joins all items of a list into one string, with `sep` between them. The items must be strings or numbers.
`print(t)` does not show the items of a table. It prints the word `table` and a memory address, which changes from run to run. Use `table.concat` or a loop to see the items.

card: `local t = {10, 20, 30}`; `t[1]` is the first item
`#t` is the length; `t[#t]` is the last item
`for i, v in ipairs(t) do ... end`
`table.insert(t, v)`, `table.insert(t, 1, v)`, `table.remove(t)`
`table.concat(t, ", ")` joins the items into a string

exercises.explain: The first index is `1`, so `t[2]` is the second item: `10`.

exercises.explain: `#t` gives the number of items in the list: four.

exercises.statement: In Lua, the first item of a list has the index `0`.
exercises.explain: Lua lists start at index `1`. `t[0]` is `nil` in a list that you create with braces.

exercises.explain: `ipairs` gives the index and the value of each item, in order.

table.insert(t, "x")

table.insert(t, 1, "z")
print(table.concat(t, "-"))
exercises.explain: `x` and `y` are added at the end. Then `z` goes to index `1`, and the others move up.

print(sum)
exercises.explain: The loop adds index times value: `1 * 4 + 2 * 5 + 3 * 6` is `4 + 10 + 18`, which is `32`.

units.title: Tables as dictionaries and objects
units.summary: Store values under keys, loop over them with pairs, put tables inside tables, and give tables their own methods with a colon.

lesson.md: A table can also store values under names, called **keys**. Write `key = value` inside the braces. You read a value with a dot, `t.key`, or with brackets and a string, `t["key"]`. A table like this works as a **dictionary**.

lesson.code:
local person = {name = "Ana", age = 30}
print(person.name)
print(person["age"])
print(person.email)

lesson.md: Assign a value to a key to add or change it. Assign `nil` to remove the key. Brackets also work with a key in a variable: `t[k]`.

lesson.code:
local stock = {apples = 5}
stock.pears = 3
stock.apples = stock.apples - 1
local fruit = "pears"
print(stock.apples)
print(stock[fruit])
stock.pears = nil
print(stock.pears)

lesson.md: `#t` only counts list items, which have the indexes `1`, `2`, `3` and so on. For a table with keys such as `name`, `#t` gives `0`.

`pairs(t)` visits every key and its value: `for key, value in pairs(t) do`. The order is not defined, and it can differ from the order in your code. Use `pairs` when the order does not matter, for example for a sum or a count.

lesson.code:
local scores = {ana = 12, ben = 8, cleo = 15}
local total = 0
local count = 0
for _, points in pairs(scores) do
    total = total + points
    count = count + 1
end
print(count)
print(total)

lesson.md: A value in a table can be another table. This lets you describe structured data, for example a game character with a position and a list of items. Chain dots and brackets to reach the inner values.

A function stored in a table is a **method**. Write `function account:deposit(n)` with a colon `:` to create one. Inside the method, `self` is the table that the method belongs to. Call it with a colon too: `account:deposit(50)` is short for `account.deposit(account, 50)`.
Strings have methods too: `s:upper()` is the same as `string.upper(s)`, and `s:sub(1, 3)` is the same as `string.sub(s, 1, 3)`.

card: `local p = {name = "Ana", age = 30}`
`p.name` or `p["name"]` reads a value; `p.age = nil` removes it
`for k, v in pairs(t) do ... end` visits all keys, in no fixed order
`function obj:move() ... self ... end`, then `obj:move()`
`s:upper()` is the same as `string.upper(s)`

p.y = p.x * 2

exercises.explain: `word:upper()` is the same as `string.upper(word)`. Then `..` adds the `!`.

exercises.code:
local t = {a = 5, b = 7, c = 1}
local n = 0
for _, v in pairs(t) do
    if v > 2 then
        n = n + 1
    end
end
print(n)
exercises.explain: The loop visits all three values in some order. Only `5` and `7` are greater than `2`, so `n` is `2` in any order.
